attribution.note: Marcus's own evaluative sentence in his own post. The Senate words he quotes are Altman's and serve only as a factual premise.

semantics.note: 'Very far cry' is a judgment about how far apart the two statements are. 'Inconsistent' is stronger and reads as a contradiction. The core is an evaluative contrast, not a checkable observation. Only the embedded Senate quotation can be checked.

contract.note: The contract rightly treats the comparison as evaluative, with no objective threshold, and separates out the checkable Senate premise. That is fair to the speaker's words.

evidence.note: The official hearing record confirms Altman said creators deserve control, so the quoted premise is accurate. It cannot settle how far the TED reply departed from it.
A secondary transcript of the TED exchange. It shows general remarks on consent and payment alongside the curt opening reply. Relevant to the comparison but cannot settle a judgment of degree.

reviews.rationale: The quoted Senate premise is accurate (e1). But 'very far cry' judges the distance between a stated principle and a later reply, and no fact can settle it. Altman's later general remarks (e2) cut both ways. The evaluative claim cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps both 'zero responsibility' and the 'appears to be' hedge on infringement. It is an observation about the TED reply.

contract.note: The plain reading is no acceptance of fault and no remedy for the specific Peanuts image. That is the ordinary meaning of taking zero responsibility, and it is not stretched either way.

evidence.note: The transcript shows a dismissive opening and then general remarks on creativity, inspiration and possible new business models. There is no acceptance of fault and no remedy for the image.
Contemporary report of Altman expressing empathy and floating an opt-in payment idea. This is general concern, not responsibility for the specific image.

reviews.rationale: Across the copyright exchange, Altman deflects, then speaks generally about creativity and future payment models. He never accepts fault for the Peanuts image or commits to any remedy (e1). His empathy and payment remarks (e2) are general and do not count as responsibility for that image.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the hedges 'appeared to be' and 'presumably'. The firm part is that an OpenAI system generated an image that looked like Peanuts. Licensing is only presumed, so under policy it is not scored.

contract.note: The support condition demands reliable evidence that the use was unlicensed. Marcus only presumed that, so the contract converts a hedge into a firm commitment. A fair reading scores only the generation and Peanuts-appearance part.

evidence.note: The transcript shows Anderson saying he asked 'it' to imagine Charlie Brown and showing the result. He then said it looked like IP theft and that OpenAI had no Peanuts deal. This supports generation and Peanuts appearance, not licensing status.

reviews.rationale: The firm part holds: Anderson showed a Charlie Brown piece generated by OpenAI's model and described it as looking like IP theft (e1). Marcus hedged licensing with 'presumably', so it is not scored, and the contract is unfair for requiring proof of it. No evidence of any licence was found.
